choices.text: Lead with the 8:20 a.m. O'Hare nonstop at $318, while retaining the evening nonstop as the lower-cost alternative.
Lead with the 5:40 p.m. Midway nonstop at $281, while retaining the morning nonstop as the earlier alternative.
Lead with the 12:10 p.m. O'Hare one-stop at $266, while retaining the evening nonstop as the simpler alternative.
Lead with the 6:35 a.m. Midway one-stop at $247, while retaining the O'Hare nonstop as the simpler alternative.

candidate.difficulty_rationale: A and B are deliberately balanced: A follows Marcus's longitudinal departure-period policy, while B saves $37 and uses the more convenient airport. Generic travel utility does not uniquely rank them. D is a near-miss that technically leaves in the morning but overweights that feature despite a connection and an unusually early start.
candidate.gold_action: Present the 8:20 a.m. outbound first and keep the cheaper evening nonstop visible as the main tradeoff.
candidate.label_rationale: This is an outbound solo work flight, and the review schedule does not require another departure period. Marcus's durable policy therefore controls presentation order: a workable morning departure should lead. The modest fare and airport-access advantages of B remain worth showing but do not displace the default ordering.
candidate.query: Marcus is traveling alone from Chicago to Phoenix for a work review that starts at 1:00 p.m. Tuesday. He can travel Monday, has no Monday commitments, and either airport is workable. The 8:20 a.m. nonstop from O'Hare is $318 and normally takes 55 minutes to reach; the 5:40 p.m. nonstop from Midway is $281 and normally takes 30 minutes to reach. Both use the same cabin and baggage rules, and either gets him there with ample rest. Two additional workable flights are listed below. No booking is requested. Which option should the planner lead with?

leakage_signals: The query explicitly neutralizes schedule, cabin, baggage, and rest differences, which makes the stated fare and airport-access advantages sufficient to select B.
The wording foregrounds the two nonstop options and labels the other flights only through their choices, but this is not necessary to resolve the comparison.
query_only_verdict.rationale: The Midway nonstop is $37 cheaper, requires 25 fewer minutes of normal airport travel, has the same cabin and baggage rules, and still provides ample rest before Tuesday's meeting. With no Monday commitments or stated preference for arriving earlier, the O'Hare flight's morning timing does not offset B's concrete price and access advantages. The one-stop options save more money but add routing complexity and do not dominate B.

choices.text: Present the 9:05 a.m. nonstop from the secondary airport at $402 first; keep the evening nonstop as the convenience-and-price alternative.
Present the 6:15 p.m. nonstop from the usual airport at $366 first; keep the morning nonstop as the earlier alternative.
Present the 1:10 p.m. nonstop from the usual airport at $388 first; keep the evening nonstop as the cheaper alternative.
Present the 7:00 a.m. one-stop from the usual airport at $331 first; keep the afternoon nonstop as the simpler alternative.

candidate.difficulty_rationale: A and B remain tied on generic grounds because A matches the durable timing policy while B is cheaper and departs from the more convenient airport. D is the near-miss: it notices the morning signal but chooses a connection solely because it is earlier and cheaper, adding a routing disadvantage that Marcus's policy does not require.
candidate.gold_action: Transfer the established outbound solo-work timing policy to the new international route and lead with the 9:05 a.m. nonstop.
candidate.label_rationale: The destination and border crossing are new, but the relevant scope is unchanged: Marcus is choosing an outbound flight for solo work, and the presentation schedule does not force a different period. The morning default transfers across route context; it does not imply that the farther airport or higher fare should be hidden.
candidate.query: Marcus is flying alone for work to Montreal for a supplier presentation at 10:00 a.m. Wednesday. He will travel Tuesday, and the team has confirmed that all four options leave enough time for customs, ground transport, and sleep. A secondary airport is about 25 minutes farther from him than his usual airport. Which itinerary should be presented first, with the others kept as alternatives?

choices.text: Lead with the 8:40 a.m. nonstop at $382 on the nonpreferred carrier; show the evening preferred-carrier flight as the savings option.
Lead with the 5:50 p.m. nonstop at $354 on the preferred carrier; show the morning nonstop as the earlier option.
Lead with the 12:30 p.m. nonstop at $365 on the preferred carrier; show the morning nonstop as the earlier option.
Lead with the 6:15 a.m. basic-economy nonstop at $329 on the preferred carrier; show the 8:40 a.m. flight as the flexible option.

candidate.difficulty_rationale: B is a strong generic choice because it is cheaper, nonstop, and on the preferred carrier; A is also nonstop but costs more and earns no meaningful loyalty advantage. Only the longitudinal policy uniquely breaks that tie. D is a near-miss that follows the morning part of the policy while ignoring the avoidable basic-economy restriction.
candidate.gold_action: Resolve the soft carrier and fare advantages in favor of the established morning-departure ordering, while retaining the evening preferred-carrier option.
candidate.label_rationale: The company carrier is preferred rather than required, the status benefit is immaterial, and the workshop imposes no departure-period constraint. Marcus's primary personal policy therefore breaks the otherwise reasonable tradeoff in favor of presenting A first.
candidate.query: For a solo work trip to Dallas, Marcus can leave Thursday for a client workshop beginning Friday at 11:00 a.m. All four flights satisfy company policy and provide adequate arrival buffer. The evening and midday flights are on the company's preferred carrier, but Marcus has not stated a personal airline preference. The qualifying-point differences are too small to change his status. Which flight should lead the comparison?

choices.text: Put the 8:35 a.m. nonstop at $321 first, with the 5:55 p.m. nonstop retained as the lower-cost alternative.
Put the 5:55 p.m. nonstop at $292 first, with the 8:35 a.m. nonstop retained as the earlier alternative.
Put the 12:20 p.m. nonstop at $277 first, with the evening nonstop retained as the later alternative.
Put the 6:25 a.m. one-stop at $249 first, with the 8:35 a.m. nonstop retained as the simpler alternative.

candidate.difficulty_rationale: A and B trade the persistent policy against recency, a $29 saving, and a later departure; the query alone does not reveal whether the prior evening choice was a new rule or a one-trip exception. The history resolves that ambiguity. D is the near-miss that recognizes the durable morning signal but applies it mechanically to a less convenient connection.
candidate.gold_action: Treat the logged evening departure as a trip-specific exception, not a revised default, and lead with the 8:35 a.m. nonstop.
candidate.label_rationale: The evening operations departure was explicitly limited to a trip whose inspection timing mattered more than the default. This new outbound solo work trip has no corresponding schedule pressure, so the durable morning ordering resumes.
candidate.query: The most recent solo operations itinerary in Marcus's trip log used an evening outbound. He is now planning a separate solo work trip to Portland for a strategy session at 11:00 a.m. Monday. He can fly Sunday, has no Sunday commitments, and every listed flight arrives with adequate time for dinner and sleep. Which option should the planner put first?

choices.text: Keep the 5:05 and 8:15 nonstops as co-leads and ask Marcus to choose between earlier arrival and $64 savings.
Lead with the 5:05 nonstop as the earliest allowed departure, keeping the 8:15 nonstop as the cheaper backup.
Lead with the 8:15 nonstop for the $64 savings, keeping the 5:05 nonstop as the earlier-arrival backup.
Lead with the 4:40 connection for the $81 savings, keeping the 8:15 nonstop as the simpler backup.

candidate.difficulty_rationale: A and B are both defensible planning actions from the query alone: B gets Marcus in earlier, while A preserves neutrality between a meaningful arrival advantage and a meaningful saving. The history makes A uniquely appropriate because it supports the exception but no fallback ordering. B is the near-miss that incorrectly translates the usual default into 'choose the earliest available flight.'
candidate.gold_action: Honor the current trip's after-4:30 requirement, avoid inventing a preference among nonmorning periods, and ask Marcus to resolve the remaining cost-versus-arrival tradeoff.
candidate.label_rationale: The current timing requirement displaces the usual departure-period default. Marcus's history establishes no reusable fallback for cases in which morning is unavailable, so the planner should not convert that default into an unsupported rule favoring the earliest, cheapest, or latest evening option.
candidate.query: Marcus is flying alone for a work inspection and has said he must finish a local all-hands meeting at 3:30 p.m. Tuesday before leaving. Airport travel makes 4:30 p.m. the earliest acceptable departure. A 5:05 p.m. nonstop costs $319 and arrives at 6:40; an 8:15 p.m. nonstop costs $255 and arrives at 9:50. A 4:40 p.m. connection costs $238 and arrives at 9:15, while a 10:00 p.m. refundable nonstop costs $365 and arrives at 11:35. The inspection begins Wednesday morning, and all four options provide the required overnight buffer. What should the planner do next?

choices.text: Lead with the 11:20 a.m. nonstop at $304, keeping the 12:15 p.m. nonstop as the closest lower-cost alternative.
Lead with the 12:15 p.m. nonstop at $282, keeping the 11:20 a.m. nonstop as the slightly earlier alternative.
Lead with the 7:05 a.m. one-stop at $247, keeping the 11:20 a.m. flight as the nonstop alternative.
Lead with the 4:50 p.m. nonstop at $271, keeping the 12:15 p.m. flight as the earlier alternative.

candidate.difficulty_rationale: The 55-minute difference is intentionally small, while B has a modest fare advantage, so generic reasoning cannot determine whether the clock boundary or savings matters more to Marcus. C is a near-miss that matches the broad period but sacrifices nonstop routing to maximize price and earliness beyond what the policy supports.
candidate.gold_action: Use the established departure-period policy to break the narrow 11:20-versus-12:15 tradeoff and present the 11:20 a.m. nonstop first.
candidate.label_rationale: This is an unconstrained outbound solo work decision. Although the two leading nonstops are close in clock time and B is $22 cheaper, A remains within Marcus's durable preferred period and should be ordered first.
candidate.query: Marcus is traveling alone for work to Salt Lake City for meetings that begin the following morning. He has no commitments on the travel day. The two closest nonstops leave only 55 minutes apart: one departs at 11:20 a.m. for $304, and the other at 12:15 p.m. for $282. The same airport, cabin, baggage rules, and ground time apply. A 7:05 a.m. one-stop is $247, and a 4:50 p.m. nonstop is $271. Which option should lead?

choices.text: Lead with Package A, emphasizing its 8:15 a.m. nonstop outbound and retaining Package B as the opposite timing pattern.
Lead with Package B, emphasizing its 9:05 a.m. return and retaining Package A as the opposite timing pattern.
Lead with Package C, emphasizing its lower total fare and retaining Package A as the earlier-outbound pattern.
Lead with Package D, emphasizing its lowest total fare and retaining Package B as the all-nonstop pattern.

candidate.difficulty_rationale: A and B are nearly equal in price and invert the morning/evening pattern across outbound and return, making them generically tied. The history is necessary to identify which leg the policy governs. B is the strongest near-miss because it follows the remembered time-of-day signal on the wrong leg; D also has a morning outbound but introduces a connection and a much earlier departure.
candidate.gold_action: Apply the remembered timing policy to the outbound leg, not the return, and lead with the package containing the 8:15 a.m. nonstop outbound.
candidate.label_rationale: Marcus's durable policy governs the outbound flight for solo work travel when the meeting schedule is neutral. It does not establish a matching preference for morning returns. A therefore follows the applicable policy, while B's morning return is irrelevant to the remembered scope.
candidate.query: For a new solo work trip, Marcus is comparing complete outbound-and-return packages rather than isolated flights. Meetings start Tuesday afternoon and end Friday at noon, so every package fits the schedule. Package A has an 8:15 a.m. Monday outbound and a 6:40 p.m. Friday return for $612. Package B has a 5:45 p.m. Monday outbound and a 9:05 a.m. Friday return for $603. Package C has a 12:10 p.m. Monday outbound and the 6:40 p.m. return for $584. Package D has a 6:30 a.m. Monday one-stop outbound and the 9:05 a.m. return for $548. All flights except D's outbound are nonstop. Which package should lead the comparison?

leakage_signals: The statement that every package fits the schedule suppresses feasibility as a differentiator and directs comparison toward fare, routing, and timing quality.

A 9:05 a.m. Friday return would conflict with meetings ending Friday at noon; the assertion that every package fits is internally suspicious and may indicate an omitted p.m. designation or synthetic wording cue.
Choice C's wording highlights its lower total fare while pairing it against A's merely earlier outbound, closely reflecting the generic dominance implied by the query.
query_only_verdict.rationale: Package C is the lowest-priced all-nonstop package and keeps the later 6:40 p.m. Friday return. It costs less than A while differing only by a later Monday outbound, which the query says fits the schedule; it costs less than B while retaining an all-nonstop itinerary; and D's additional $36 savings requires a one-stop 6:30 a.m. outbound and the less favorable return pattern. C is therefore the strongest generic balance without assuming a personal timing preference.

choices.text: Keep the 5:05 and 8:15 nonstops together at the top and ask Marcus to choose between the earlier arrival and the $64 savings.
Lead with the 5:05 nonstop as the earliest feasible departure, keeping the 8:15 nonstop as the savings alternative.
Lead with the 8:15 nonstop as the cheaper departure, keeping the 5:05 nonstop as the earlier-arrival alternative.
Lead with the 4:40 p.m. connection at $238, keeping the 8:15 nonstop as the simpler alternative.

candidate.difficulty_rationale: A and B are both reasonable from the trip facts: asking preserves neutrality, while B buys more destination time. The history is needed to show both that the normal default yields to this constraint and that it must not be transformed into an unsupported 'earliest available' rule.
candidate.gold_action: Honor the current trip's timing constraint, avoid inventing an ordering among nonmorning periods, and ask Marcus to resolve the balanced cost-versus-arrival tradeoff.
candidate.label_rationale: The all-hands meeting displaces Marcus's usual outbound-work default, just as the inspection schedule did in the prior exception episode. His history establishes no reusable fallback favoring the earliest or cheapest flight when morning travel is unavailable, so A preserves the unresolved tradeoff.
candidate.query: Marcus is flying alone for a work inspection and must finish a local all-hands meeting at 3:30 p.m. Tuesday before leaving. Allowing for airport travel, 4:30 p.m. is the earliest feasible departure. A 5:05 p.m. nonstop costs $319 and arrives at 6:40 p.m.; an 8:15 p.m. nonstop costs $255 and arrives at 9:50 p.m. The earlier flight provides more time to settle in, while the later flight saves $64. Both have the same fare conditions and provide the required overnight buffer before Wednesday's inspection. A cheaper connection and a late refundable flight are also available. What should the planner do next?

leakage_signals: Choice A uniquely offers preference elicitation rather than assuming whether time or money matters more; this wording cue is sufficient to identify the best next action.
query_only_verdict.rationale: The two feasible nonstops present a material but unresolved tradeoff between a 3-hour-10-minute earlier arrival and $64 in savings. Asking Marcus to choose between those outcomes is the only option that avoids inventing a preference while keeping both strong itineraries at the top.
